fatal_errors: The hypothesis assigns the principal control to differential diffusion barriers and configurational-entropy stabilization, whereas the target mechanism is active, non-sluggish diffusion driven primarily by elemental surface-energy differences, especially Au/Cu surface segregation.
It treats strong surface-energy effects as a possible exception even though they are central to the target phenomenon.

Testing mainly at 473 and 1923 K misses the observed onset above approximately 673 K and the decisive 973 K melting/evaporation regime; at 1923 K, loss or melting of these nanoparticles would confound a segregation-only test.
explanation: The response correctly identifies temperature-activated diffusion as a mediator and predicts loss of chemical homogeneity at elevated temperature, so it captures part of the broad phenomenon. However, it does not reconstruct the AuCoCuNiPt sub-10 nm system, the vacuum ramp to 973 K, or the stepped in situ STEM/EDS and molecular-dynamics analysis. Its mechanism misses preferential Au/Cu segregation caused by low surface energies, shape-enhanced diffusion, and subsequent shell melting and evaporation. It also omits the predicted disappearance of 2–4 nm particles, distribution broadening, approximately 22% size reduction, and elliptical-to-spherical reshaping. The room-temperature control and microscopy/EDS/XRD measurements offer some falsifiability, but they do not isolate surface energy from diffusion-barrier effects or test the key size- and shape-dependent boundary.
